title: Reverse Engineering: the binary talks
description: strings as a baseline, compression layers to peel and XOR inside ELF sections: three binaries, three techniques.

1.title: Levels 1-3: strings, zlib and XOR
1.body:
## Level 1: the baseline

```bash
curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18111/level1.sh
strings level1.sh | grep -i "hash\|flag\|key"
# CONFIG_HASH="RkxBR3tzdHJpbmdzX2Jhc2VsaW5lX3JlfQ=="
echo "RkxBR3tz..." | base64 -d
```

`strings` extracts everything printable from the binary. 80% of early
reversing is exactly this: hardcoded passwords, C2 URLs, paths, tokens.
Before opening a disassembler, ALWAYS run strings.

## Level 2: the layer you have to peel

The script runs and says "nothing to see here". The trick is in the
payload it never executes:

```bash
curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18111/level2.py
python3 -c "
import re, base64, zlib
blob = re.search(r'_PAYLOAD = \"([^\"]+)\"', open('level2.py').read()).group(1)
print(zlib.decompress(base64.b64decode(blob)).decode())
"
```

Real malware packs its stages like this: base64 → zlib → XOR → sometimes
several rounds. Each layer is peeled off in the reverse order it was applied. In
CTFs, the zlib magic (`78 9c`) in a dump is the sign that it's time to
decompress.

## Level 3: XOR in the ELF

```bash
curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18111/level3.bin
file level3.bin          # ELF 64-bit
xxd level3.bin | head -4 # look at the real header
```

`strings` can't see the flag because it's XORed. A single-byte XOR has
256 possible keys — you brute-force it in a second:

```python
data = open('level3.bin','rb').read()
for key in range(256):
    dec = bytes(b ^ key for b in data)
    if b'FLAG{' in dec:
        print(f'key=0x{key:02x}:', dec[dec.index(b"FLAG{"):].split(b"}")[0].decode() + "}")
```

This single-byte XOR brute force solves more CTFs than anyone will
admit. When the key is multi-byte, you move on to frequency analysis
or to hunting for the key material in .data (the cryptography room's prologue
applies directly).

## The kit you'll build up

strings → xxd/od → python one-liners → objdump/readelf (sections,
symbols) → ltrace/strace (what it calls) → gdb (breakpoints) → Ghidra
(decompiling). Each level of this room is one rung on that ladder.

reverse-engineering-t01-q01.prompt: Download level1.sh. A perfectly normal healthcheck with an odd CONFIG_HASH. Submit the flag.
reverse-engineering-t01-q01.hint: curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18111/level1.sh && strings level1.sh | grep CONFIG — then base64 -d

reverse-engineering-t01-q02.prompt: level2.py runs without errors and prints nothing useful. The compressed _PAYLOAD hides the flag. Submit it.
reverse-engineering-t01-q02.hint: import zlib, base64; zlib.decompress(base64.b64decode(blob)) — running the script does NOT reveal it: you have to read the code

reverse-engineering-t01-q03.prompt: level3.bin is a real ELF (magic 7f 45 4c 46). Its .data section stores the flag XORed with one byte. Submit it.
reverse-engineering-t01-q03.hint: python: bytes(b ^ 0x5A for b in open('level3.bin','rb').read()) and look for FLAG{ — why 0x5A? try it, or brute-force the byte with a 1..255 loop
